draft.title: Militarism in Japan
card: Militarism is the belief that the armed forces should have great influence over a country's government and that military strength should shape its policies. In the 1930s Japan's army and navy came to hold this kind of influence.

Japan's economy was hit hard by the Depression, and many Japanese people lost faith in elected politicians. Army officers promised strong leadership and expansion abroad to gain land, markets and resources.
In 1931 the Japanese army in Manchuria, in north-east China, staged an incident on a railway it controlled and used it as an excuse to take over the region. Civilian leaders in Tokyo did not stop it.
Army officers and their supporters killed several politicians in the 1930s, and military figures came to dominate cabinets. In 1937 Japan launched a full invasion of China.
draft.remember: In 1930s Japan the army gained control of the government, and that control drove expansion into Manchuria and China.

a.q: Which description best fits militarism in 1930s Japan?
opts: The armed forces held great influence over government policy
Elected politicians controlled the army through parliament
The emperor was removed and replaced by a military ruler
Japan avoided foreign conflict to rebuild its economy
a.why: Militarism means the armed forces have great influence over government and policy, and in the 1930s the army and navy came to hold it. Civilian politicians did not control the army: in Manchuria the army acted without their approval.
a.clue: Think about who made the decisions, the army or the politicians.

b.q: Japanese army officers in Manchuria staged a railway incident in 1931 and then took over the region, while the government in Tokyo did not stop them. What does this show?
opts: The army could act with little control from civilian leaders
The government in Tokyo had planned the invasion in detail
Japan's economy no longer needed new land or resources
China had already attacked Japan in Manchuria first
b.why: The army used a staged incident as an excuse and the civilian government did not stop it, which shows the army's growing power. The incident was staged by the army, so it was not a real Chinese attack that started the conflict.
b.clue: Who acted, and who failed to stop them?

a.best: The armed forces held great influence over government policy

b.best: The army could act with little control from civilian leaders

problems.detail: The remember line says the army 'gained control of the government' and that 'that control drove expansion into Manchuria'. The card is more careful. It says the army and navy came to hold great influence, and that military figures dominated cabinets later in the 1930s. In 1931 the Manchurian takeover was the army acting on its own while civilian leaders failed to stop it, not the army using control of the government. The line overstates the card and blurs the order of events.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the facts check out: the Mukden Incident in 1931, the assassinations of politicians, and the 1937 invasion. The remember line overstates the card by saying the army controlled the government and that this control drove the 1931 takeover of Manchuria, which the card presents as the army acting without civilian control.
